cards.front: For ordinary rounding, what inequality form is used for an error interval?
Why is the upper bound excluded in normal rounding?
cards.back: It would round up to the next answer.

options.text: It would round up to the next answer.
options.explanation: The upper bound is exactly halfway between consecutive rounded answers. Under ordinary rounding, this value rounds up, so it belongs to the next interval.

options.text: It would round down to the previous answer.
options.explanation: This confuses the upper and lower boundaries. The upper bound rounds up to the next answer, which is why it is excluded from the interval.

options.text: It would round back to the same answer.
options.explanation: Treating the upper bound as part of the interval creates overlapping answers. It rounds up to the next answer, so the upper inequality must be strict.

options.text: It would fall below the lower bound.
options.explanation: The upper bound cannot fall below the lower bound; they are opposite endpoints. It is excluded because it rounds up to the next answer.

cards.front: For rounding, find bounds by going [ ___ ] and [ ___ ] from the rounded value.
cards.back: For rounding, find bounds by going half a step down and half a step up from the rounded value.

options.text: For rounding, find bounds by going half a step down and half a step up from the rounded value.
options.explanation: Rounding boundaries lie halfway between consecutive possible rounded values. Therefore, subtract half the rounding step for the lower bound and add half for the upper bound.

options.text: For rounding, find bounds by going half a step up and half a step down from the rounded value.
options.explanation: This swaps the directions of the bounds, placing the lower bound above the value. Go half a step down first and half a step up second.

options.text: For rounding, find bounds by going one full step down and one full step up from the rounded value.
options.explanation: Using a full step makes the interval twice as wide as it should be. Rounding boundaries are half a step down and half a step up.

options.text: For rounding, find bounds by going half a step down and one full step up from the rounded value.
options.explanation: The lower adjustment is correct, but the upper adjustment uses a full step. Both boundaries must be exactly half a rounding step from the rounded value.

cards.front: Correct to the nearest kg, cm or m has step size [ ___ ] and half-step [ ___ ].
cards.back: Correct to the nearest kg, cm or m has step size 1 whole unit and half-step 0.5 units.

options.text: Correct to the nearest kg, cm or m has step size 1 whole unit and half-step 0.5 units.
options.explanation: Consecutive whole-number measurements differ by one unit. The rounding boundaries are halfway between them, so the half-step is $0.5$ units.

options.text: Correct to the nearest kg, cm or m has step size 0.5 units and half-step 0.25 units.
options.explanation: This incorrectly treats half a unit as the gap between consecutive whole-number answers. The step is $1$ whole unit and its half-step is $0.5$ units.

options.text: Correct to the nearest kg, cm or m has step size 1 whole unit and half-step 1 whole unit.
options.explanation: The step size is correct, but the half-step has not been divided by two. Half of $1$ whole unit is $0.5$ units.

options.text: Correct to the nearest kg, cm or m has step size 2 whole units and half-step 1 whole unit.
options.explanation: This doubles the gap between possible rounded measurements. Nearest-unit answers increase by $1$ whole unit, giving a half-step of $0.5$ units.

cards.front: 18 kg correct to the nearest kg: write the error interval for mass $m$.

options.explanation: Rounding to the nearest kilogram has a half-step of $0.5$ kg. Subtracting and adding $0.5$ gives bounds of $17.5$ and $18.5$.
This uses a full kilogram on each side rather than half a kilogram. The correct bounds are $17.5 \le m < 18.5$.
The endpoint inclusion is reversed. A mass of $17.5$ kg rounds to $18$ kg, while $18.5$ kg rounds to $19$ kg, giving $17.5 \le m < 18.5$.
This starts at the rounded value instead of half a unit below it. The interval must extend from $17.5$ kg up to, but not including, $18.5$ kg.

cards.front: Rounded to 1 decimal place: step size [ ___ ], half-step [ ___ ].
cards.back: Rounded to 1 decimal place: step size 0.1, half-step 0.05.

options.text: Rounded to 1 decimal place: step size 0.1, half-step 0.05.
options.explanation: Adjacent numbers to one decimal place differ by $0.1$. Dividing this rounding step by two gives the half-step, $0.05$.

options.text: Rounded to 1 decimal place: step size 0.01, half-step 0.005.
options.explanation: These values apply to rounding to two decimal places, not one. For one decimal place, the step is $0.1$ and the half-step is $0.05$.

options.text: Rounded to 1 decimal place: step size 0.1, half-step 0.1.
options.explanation: The step size is correct, but it has not been halved. Half of $0.1$ is $0.05$, so that is the required half-step.

options.text: Rounded to 1 decimal place: step size 1, half-step 0.5.
options.explanation: These values apply to rounding to the nearest whole number. One-decimal-place values differ by $0.1$, so their half-step is $0.05$.

cards.front: A number rounds to 9.6 to 1 decimal place. What is the error interval for $y$?

options.explanation: The step for one decimal place is $0.1$, so the half-step is $0.05$. Subtracting and adding $0.05$ to $9.6$ gives the stated interval.
This uses a full step of $0.1$ on both sides, making the interval twice as wide. The correct half-step is $0.05$, giving $9.55 \le y < 9.65$.
This reverses the endpoint inclusion. The lower bound $9.55$ rounds to $9.6$, while the upper bound $9.65$ rounds to $9.7$.
This uses a half-step of $0.005$, which applies to two decimal places. For one decimal place, use $0.05$, giving $9.55 \le y < 9.65$.

cards.front: Rounded to 2 decimal places: step size [ ___ ], half-step [ ___ ].
cards.back: Rounded to 2 decimal places: step size 0.01, half-step 0.005.

options.text: Rounded to 2 decimal places: step size 0.01, half-step 0.005.
options.explanation: Adjacent values to two decimal places differ by one hundredth, or $0.01$. Half of this step is $0.005$.

options.text: Rounded to 2 decimal places: step size 0.1, half-step 0.05.
options.explanation: These values apply to one decimal place, not two. For two decimal places, the step is $0.01$ and the half-step is $0.005$.

options.text: Rounded to 2 decimal places: step size 0.01, half-step 0.01.
options.explanation: The step size is right, but it has not been divided by two. Half of $0.01$ is $0.005$, which determines the bounds.

options.text: Rounded to 2 decimal places: step size 0.001, half-step 0.0005.
options.explanation: These values apply to three decimal places. Two-decimal-place answers increase in steps of $0.01$, so the correct half-step is $0.005$.

cards.front: A number rounds to 1.34 to 2 decimal places. What is the error interval for $x$?

options.explanation: Rounding to 2 decimal places uses a half-step of $0.005$. The lower bound is included, while the upper bound is excluded because it rounds to $1.35$.
This uses a full step of $0.01$ on either side instead of a half-step. The correct bounds are $1.335$ and $1.345$, giving $1.335 \le x < 1.345$.
The endpoint signs are reversed. $1.335$ is included because it rounds to $1.34$, but $1.345$ is excluded because it rounds to $1.35$.
This uses a half-step of $0.0005$, appropriate for 3 decimal places. For 2 decimal places the half-step is $0.005$, so the bounds are $1.335$ and $1.345$.

cards.front: Why is $1.345$ not included for numbers rounding to 1.34 to 2 decimal places?

options.explanation: The third decimal digit is $5$, so the second decimal digit rounds up. Therefore $1.345$ rounds to $1.35$ and is the excluded upper bound.
This incorrectly rounds a final $5$ down. Using the usual GCSE rule, the hundredths digit rounds up, so $1.345$ rounds to $1.35$.
Rounding up changes the hundredths digit from $4$ to $5$, not to $6$. Therefore $1.345$ rounds to $1.35$, making it the excluded upper bound.
This leaves the number unrounded. To 2 decimal places, the third decimal digit $5$ makes the hundredths digit round up, so the result is $1.35$.

cards.front: Significant figures are counted from the first [ ___ ] digit.
cards.back: Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit.

options.explanation: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are not significant. Counting begins at the first digit that is not zero, so the required term is non-zero.
Leading zeros are not significant because they only show place value. Significant figures begin at the first non-zero digit, such as the $4$ in $0.00472$.
The decimal point does not determine where significant figures begin. Counting starts at the first non-zero digit, whether the number is greater than or less than one.
Digits themselves are not classified as positive for this rule, and the sign of the number is irrelevant. Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit.

cards.front: For significant-figure rounding, what decides the half-step?
cards.back: Half the place value of the last significant figure.

options.text: Half the place value of the last significant figure.
options.explanation: Adjacent rounded values differ by the place value of the last significant figure. Each error bound lies halfway between them, so the half-step is half that place value.

options.text: The full place value of the last significant figure.
options.explanation: Using the full place value makes the interval twice as wide as it should be. Each boundary is half a rounding unit away, so use half the place value.

options.text: Twice the place value of the last significant figure.
options.explanation: Doubling the place value greatly overestimates the rounding interval. The boundaries are halfway to the adjacent rounded values, so use half the final significant figure’s place value.

options.text: Half the rounded value of the last significant figure.
options.explanation: The half-step depends on the position of the last significant figure, not half of its numerical value. It is half the place value of that figure.

cards.front: 0.472 rounded to 3 significant figures: what half-step is used?

options.explanation: The final significant figure in $0.472$ is in the thousandths place, with place value $0.001$. Half of $0.001$ is $0.0005$.
This is half of $0.01$, treating the final significant figure as hundredths. It is actually in the thousandths place, so the correct half-step is $0.0005$.
This is half of $0.0001$, as though the number had been rounded to 4 significant figures. The final digit is thousandths, so the half-step is $0.0005$.
This is the full place value of the final significant figure rather than half of it. The thousandths place has value $0.001$, so the half-step is $0.0005$.

cards.front: 0.472 rounded to 3 significant figures: write the error interval for $x$.

options.explanation: The last significant figure is in the thousandths place, so the half-step is $0.0005$. Subtracting and adding this gives the bounds $0.4715$ and $0.4725$.
This subtracts and adds the full thousandths place value rather than half of it. Using the correct half-step $0.0005$ gives $0.4715 \le x < 0.4725$.
The endpoint signs are reversed. $0.4715$ rounds up to $0.472$ and is included, while $0.4725$ rounds up to $0.473$ and is excluded.
This uses a half-step of $0.00005$, appropriate when rounding to 4 significant figures. For 3 significant figures the half-step is $0.0005$, giving bounds $0.4715$ and $0.4725$.

cards.front: 7000 rounded to 1 significant figure: what column is the 7 in?

options.explanation: In $7000$, the digit $7$ represents seven thousand, so it occupies the thousands column. It is therefore the first and only non-zero significant figure.
The hundreds column is occupied by the first zero, not the $7$. The digit $7$ represents $7000$, so it is in the thousands column.
The tens column is the second zero from the right. The digit $7$ has a value of seven thousand, so it belongs in the thousands column.
The units column contains the final zero on the right. The digit $7$ represents seven lots of one thousand, placing it in the thousands column.

cards.front: 7000 rounded to 1 significant figure: write the error interval for $x$.

options.explanation: The $7$ is in the thousands column, so the rounding unit is $1000$ and the half-step is $500$. This gives $6500 \le x < 7500$.
This uses the full rounding unit of $1000$ on each side rather than the half-step. Using $500$ gives the correct interval $6500 \le x < 7500$.
The endpoint signs are reversed. $6500$ rounds up to $7000$ and is included, while $7500$ rounds up to $8000$ and must be excluded.
These bounds treat $7000$ as rounded to the nearest whole number. Rounding to 1 significant figure uses a half-step of $500$, giving $6500 \le x < 7500$.

cards.front: Truncation means [ ___ ] extra digits without [ ___ ].
cards.back: Truncation means cutting off extra digits without rounding up.

options.text: Truncation means cutting off extra digits without rounding up.
options.explanation: Truncation removes all digits beyond the required place value and leaves the final retained digit unchanged, rather than increasing it according to the next digit.

options.text: Truncation means cutting off extra digits without rounding down.
options.explanation: Truncation is sometimes confused with rounding down, but it simply cuts off extra digits without rounding up or otherwise changing the last retained digit.

options.text: Truncation means rounding off extra digits without rounding up.
options.explanation: Rounding off requires considering the first discarded digit, whereas truncation means cutting off extra digits without rounding up, regardless of the discarded digits.

options.text: Truncation means cutting off extra digits without rounding to nearest.
options.explanation: Although truncation does not round to the nearest value, the precise definition is cutting off extra digits without rounding up, leaving the retained digits unchanged.

cards.front: For a positive truncated number, where does the error interval start?
cards.back: At the displayed truncated value, included.

options.text: At the displayed truncated value, included.
options.explanation: For a positive truncated number, the original value can equal the displayed value, so the interval begins there and includes that lower boundary.

options.text: At the displayed truncated value, not included.
options.explanation: Excluding the displayed value is an endpoint error. The original number may equal its truncated form, so the interval starts at the displayed truncated value, included.

options.text: At the next possible place value, included.
options.explanation: The next place-value increment is the upper boundary, not the starting point. For a positive number, the interval starts at the displayed truncated value, included.

options.text: At the halfway rounding value, included.
options.explanation: Using a halfway value confuses truncation with rounding to the nearest value. A positive truncation interval starts at the displayed truncated value itself, included.

cards.front: A positive number is truncated to 6.2 to 1 decimal place. What is the upper boundary?

options.explanation: Truncating to one decimal place retains values from 6.2 up to, but not including, 6.3; at 6.3 the displayed truncated value would change.
The value 6.25 is a rounding boundary, obtained by using half of 0.1. Truncation instead has upper boundary 6.3, which is not included.
The numerical boundary is right, but including it is an endpoint error. Exactly 6.3 truncates to 6.3, so the upper boundary is 6.3, not included.
The value 6.2 is the included lower boundary, not the upper boundary. The interval extends to 6.3, which is excluded because it truncates to 6.3.

cards.front: A number is truncated to 4.73 to 2 decimal places. What is the error interval for $x$?

options.explanation: Truncating to two decimal places keeps every value from 4.73 up to 4.74. The lower boundary is included, while 4.74 is excluded.
These are the boundaries for rounding 4.73 to two decimal places. Truncation begins at 4.73 and extends to, but does not include, 4.74.
The endpoint inequalities have been reversed. The value 4.73 can truncate to 4.73, but 4.74 cannot, so $4.73 \le x < 4.74$.
This is the interval for values that truncate to 4.72, an off-by-one place-value increment. Values truncating to 4.73 satisfy $4.73 \le x < 4.74$.
